en: How could that poor soul remain dead
And not rise back to life?
To see her Semetey,
To behold him and then die,
To turn her face toward the qibla,
And surrender her withered soul,
She began a fierce exertion.
Kanykei left her dear life
Hanging by a single thread.
The flesh of her palate clicked,
Her mouth parched and smacked with thirst,
The poor, grieving soul at life’s end—
Once they had encountered one another,
Would I not wail myself to death,
Would I not surrender my fly-like soul?
When all who grieve come together,
So this is how it must be.”
Thus the people raised an uproar,
Their hearts crushed as though by lead;
Mother and son were reunited,
They came face-to-face at that place,
A place the mighty Creator
Had truly bestowed.
Gathering the host and assembling the troops,
Stroking his white beard,
Sobbing, “O my only moon!”
Your magnanimous old Bakai
Stood there lamenting.
Surging like embers,
Burning fiercely like fire,
Your heroic grandsire Bakai
Turned his face toward the qibla,
Ready to surrender his poor life.
The old man who had suffered many torments
Could not restrain his tears:
“Alas, blue-maned leopard,
Your living form has appeared.
What more could I want in my grief?
My orphan whom I cherished,
Here, right before you,
Let me sacrifice myself for you.
Yesterday, when my bloodthirsty prince still lived,
When the towering city of Kakanchy
Lay beneath my siege,
When I was beating down
Its khans and nobles,
Did I descend upon some enchanted ridge?
Thirsting terribly in the night,
How else have I survived until now—
Did I drink the water of immortality?
While the bloodthirsty lord, her son, stood there,
She wailed, unable to reach him;
The reason for her wailing was
That she could not pass beyond
The spellbinder’s blinding sorcery.
Weeping bitterly and beating herself,
Poor, withered Kanykei stood there,
Pleading with her only cherished Semetey,
Begging Semetey.
Then Kanykei said:
“My pale-gray falcon,
My hazy, tranquil morning star,
The one for whom I braided my servant’s hair,
The one I waited so long to see.
If my racehorse dies, you are my hoof,
You are the talon of my falcon,
You are the hoof of my racehorse.
My falcon, you shall be lightning…”
His mother stood weeping,
Her heart wrung with anguish.
The blood flowing down both cheeks
Fell upon her breast.
When Kanykei stood weeping,
The birch and willow wept;
The cherished one appeared before their eyes,
And every soul who saw him wept.
The people sobbed and wept,
The newly cherished shore wept,
The precious ones wept, the lions wept,
Countless people wept in anguish,
The heavyhearted lion wept.
All who were weeping
Wept, consumed by their own sorrows.
O bereft and grieving soul of bygone days,
O never-ending tears from the eyes;
Each one weeps, consumed by grief,
Whenever sorrowful misfortune strikes.
When mother and child are overcome,
When a child meets his father again,
The dead return to life,
And the extinguished flame is kindled anew,
When our lord was gone from sight,
Our heads sank lower than a kid goat’s.
Kanchoro, whom we raised with lullabies,
Showed us the city of Alai
And wrought countless deeds, I suppose.”
The sage Bakai said this,
And stood sobbing loudly,
Lamenting with a ringing voice.
Before he had finished speaking,
The moonlike lady Aichürök,
Smiling faintly through her pallor,
Her face shining clear as a mirror,
Cried out for her betrothed,
And wept without restraint, sobbing.
She met him in sorrow and lamentation,
Sobbing and weeping, overcome.
Her black hair, untouched by a comb,
Fell apart strand by strand;
Her dear hair, long as horsehair,
Spread across her breast.
From her quail-like eyes,
Separate tears streamed;
From her blackcurrant eyes,
Tears fell in drops as heavy as a whip.
“O blue-maned lion!” she cried,
Sobbing that they had been reunited:
“My princely leopard, surpassing lion,
You increased your nobility,
But made this wretched head endure
Torment, hardship, and calamity.
The Zulpukor blade is supreme,
Yet you let Bölökbai trample it,
And, lost for sixteen years,
You made me guard the foot of the mountain.
My noble blue-maned lion,
My anguish never leaves my thoughts.
Yellowed as though with jaundice,
I endured a hundred grievous afflictions.
I preserved what was entrusted to me
Amid a hundred enemies.
Did I eat the flesh of some great bird?
Crushed and turned to embers,
From that time until this,
Parted from the great ones,
I wandered in misery and confusion—
Was this how you wished me to die?
I burned and baked, becoming an ember;
I was shattered and came to nothing.
I was a fine steed, but I wasted away;
I was a blue-maned lion, but I grew weary.
I burned away and lost
Half the youth of the blue-maned lion.
Steel softened and I became brass;
I faced many a storm,
And was gnawed and devoured by nobles.
They called me gray-bearded Bakai,
And I became a byword among cruel foes.
My wings, my pinions, and my tail
Were plucked, trimmed, and devoured.
My brain boiled where no water could reach,
And I became a barren desert where no grass grows.
Stripped of tail and mane,
I became the wild ass of that desert.
Neither dying nor vanishing, I grieved;
O bloodthirsty lion whom I cherished,
O leopard, I was parted from you.
My eyes became blood-filled sores;
I became a soul no longer needed.
I was once a proud and splendid man,
But became a stooping old man.
My waist was bent like a fox’s;
My vigor gone, my wretched soul
I burdened upon the beasts of night.
From my earliest days, I, Bakai,
Was born to be a warrior;
But when the hero vanished from sight,
I was beset by so many calamities.
My wretched soul was dragged
Like a kökbörü carcass among strongmen.
Our years stretched long in mockery.
The hero’s son Seytek.
To see his father’s face,
His fitting words came too late,
His two eyes strained into four,
Burning, seething, surging,
To his father, the bloodthirsty prince,
Noble Seytek pleaded.
If he wished his people well,
Seytek, who had remained behind,
Looked upon Semetey:
His beard was like an arrow case,
And when he looked at his mustache,
It was like the blade of an ornate sheath.
The breath that issued from his mouth
Was like a flame that ravaged a valley.
His lashes were flame, his eyes were embers;
No man possessed such fearful power.
His ferocity and lionheartedness
Surpassed the whole wide world.
My father the khan’s valor—
His face was dark, his speech fierce,
His courage unmatched, his wrath ablaze.
My leopard father was like a lion;
There is no such mortal in the world.
His round ears were like shields,
His great eyes like the Morning Star,
His aquiline nose like a mountain ridge,
The breath that issued from his mouth
Was like the wind through a palace gorge.
Whoever roused his anger,
He seemed able to devour with all his age.
Of middle height and broad of shoulder,
He bristled with boundless valor,
Like a black-mottled leopard
Rearing up beside him.
Like a short-maned gray lion
About to tear open a wound,
He made ready on every side.
A towering black camel of singular form
Pressed forward behind him.
The blessed child you bore in your womb—
You have subjected him to every trial;
The wife lovely as the promised moon,
The wise one cherished by all,
You have left a widow all these years.
Your chosen mount is the black-bay steed;
Behind you the black-faced woman laments.
From this moment take the grief-stricken woman
And bear her away at your saddle bow.
May fortune favor this fleeting world,
So we may share the ordained burden,
So we may meet and lie together,
So we may melt and know each other’s secrets,
So we may unite and journey together.
Take your poor wretch with you;
Keep me ruling in your heart,
Though you travel far on many journeys.
Gray-maned prince and leopard,
Bear me away at your saddle bow.
All my many kinds of dresses,
Though I heap them up, will not reach my neck;
Do not leave this hapless head in want,
But take me into your embrace.”
So saying, she wailed aloud,
And Aichürök sobbed and wept;
Every living soul melted,
All the sorrowful met that day,
All the dear ones sobbed,
And all who remained cried out.
The ancient cavern and the curved cliffs seemed to melt,
As parents and child were reunited.
The Black Giant and Külchoro,
And all the warriors, grew excited;
All those burdened by sorrow
Met the hero upon the open plain,
And stood there overwhelmed.
Before he had finished speaking,
The people’s thoughts were divided;
See what such a parting was like—
He had gone and encountered,
Chasing the white doe,
And truly had turned her into a cow.
My lion father had indeed
Brought the whole world under his command.
My gray-maned father stirred up strife,
